\chapter{Decidir, Coincidir, Equivocarse}
\label{ch:es-plan}
\hlchaptermodality{437}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can decide between two dates, say that one clashes, admit a mistake, say how long something takes, and name the evening meal.}

Read the notice or message this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[decidir]{decidir — to cut the question off}

\label{lesson:ES-C437-decidir}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{ofrecer}. The shop has offered you Thursday or Saturday. Say what you now have to do.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: decidir}
\textbf{decidir} — to decide. \textbf{decidirse} — to make up your mind.

\emph{Usted decide} — you decide. It is what a notice says when it has finished offering and the choice is yours.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{de-} off, plus \textbf{-cidir} from Latin \emph{caedere}, to cut. To \textbf{cut the question off}.

The same \emph{caedere} is under a family that all involve cutting something away:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{what is cut} \\
\midrule
decidir & the question \\
preciso & cut exactly to size \\
conciso & cut short \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{decidir} and \textbf{decidirse} are not the same. \emph{Decido el menú} is choosing a thing; \emph{me decido} is the inner moment when you stop hesitating. Spanish marks that difference with the reflexive, where English leans on \emph{decide} versus \emph{make up my mind}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{decidir}
  \item they offered me Thursday and I have to decide
  \item the difference between \emph{decido} and \emph{me decido}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To decide? (\textbf{decidir}.) To make up your mind? (\textbf{decidirse}.) What does the Latin piece mean? (\textbf{To cut}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[coincidir]{coincidir — to fall on the same day}

\label{lesson:ES-C437-coincidir}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{el grupo}. Say \emph{decidir}. The Tuesday group meets at the hour you already have something else. Name that problem.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: coincidir}
\textbf{coincidir} — to coincide, and in everyday use \textbf{to clash}.

\emph{Me coincide con el trabajo} — it clashes with work. That is the ordinary reason somebody gives for not taking a place.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{co-} together, plus the same \textbf{-incidir} family as \emph{decidir} — things falling together.

Your English eye can read it without help, and that is the point worth taking:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
coincidir & coincide \\
decidir & decide \\
dividir & divide \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{But the everyday meaning has drifted.} English \emph{coincide} is neutral or lucky; Spanish \textbf{coincidir}, said about a timetable, is almost always a complaint. The form is transparent and the use is not, which is exactly where a confident reader gets caught.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{coincidir}
  \item it clashes with my work
  \item the Tuesday group clashes with my class
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To clash? (\textbf{coincidir}.) What does the \emph{co-} add? (\textbf{Together}.) Is it usually good news? (\textbf{No} — about a timetable it is a complaint.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[equivocarse]{equivocarse — when two things sound the same}

\label{lesson:ES-C437-equivocarse}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{el pedido}. The restaurant has sent two salads instead of a salad and a soup. Say what they did.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: equivocarse}
\textbf{equivocarse} — to be mistaken, to get it wrong.

\emph{Nos hemos equivocado} — we have made a mistake. It is how a shop apologises without naming who is at fault.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{aequus} equal, plus \textbf{vox} voice. \emph{Equal voice} — two things that sound the same and get taken for each other.

That is a precise picture of what a mistake is, and the same two pieces give you a word you may already recognise:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{the equal voice in it} \\
\midrule
equivocarse & to confuse two things \\
equívoco & ambiguous \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{It is almost always reflexive.} You say \emph{me equivoco}, not \emph{equivoco}, because the error happens \textbf{to you} rather than being done to something else. Spanish uses that reflexive for a whole family of things that befall a person — \emph{caerse}, \emph{olvidarse}, \emph{perderse} — and it is worth noticing as a group rather than memorising one at a time.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{equivocarse}
  \item we have made a mistake with the order
  \item I was wrong
  \item what the two Latin pieces mean
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To get it wrong? (\textbf{equivocarse}.) The two pieces? (\textbf{Equal voice}.) Which form do you use? (\textbf{The reflexive} — \emph{me equivoco}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tardar]{tardar — how long a thing takes}

\label{lesson:ES-C437-tardar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{el retraso}. That lesson mentioned a second word for lateness and did not teach it. Say it if you remember; here it is either way.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: tardar}
\textbf{tardar} — to take time, to be long about something.

\emph{Tardo una hora} — it takes me an hour. \emph{¿Cuánto tarda?} — how long does it take?

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the delay and the duration}]
\textbf{el retraso} and \textbf{tardar} are not interchangeable, and the difference is worth having exactly:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{you mean} & \textbf{you say} \\
\midrule
it is later than promised & lleva retraso \\
it takes this long & tarda una hora \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

A journey that \textbf{tarda} two hours is not late — two hours is what the journey costs. A train with \textbf{retraso} has broken a promise. English blurs both into \emph{late} and \emph{takes}, and a reader who maps one to one will misread a station announcement.

Both come from \textbf{tardus}, slow, so the shared root is real and the split is recent.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tardar}
  \item how long does it take?
  \item it takes an hour and it is not late
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To take time? (\textbf{tardar}.) Later than promised? (\textbf{con retraso}.) Which one is a broken promise? (\textbf{retraso}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cenar]{cenar — the meal as a verb}

\label{lesson:ES-C437-cenar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{comer}. You can say you eat. Say that you eat \textbf{in the evening}, and notice how many words English needs.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: cenar}
\textbf{cenar} — to have dinner, to dine. \textbf{la cena} is the meal itself.

\emph{Cenamos a las nueve} — we have dinner at nine.

\begin{cousinweb}
Spanish makes a \textbf{verb out of each meal}, where English has to say \emph{have} plus a noun:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish verb} & \textbf{English needs} \\
\midrule
desayunar & to have breakfast \\
comer & to have lunch \\
cenar & to have dinner \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{comer} is the trap in that list. You already hold it as \emph{to eat}, and in Spain it also means specifically \textbf{to have lunch} — \emph{¿has comido?} at four in the afternoon is asking whether you have had lunch, not whether you have eaten anything at all today.

So the three verbs are a set, and \emph{comer} belongs to it as well as to the general sense.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cenar}
  \item we have dinner at nine
  \item the three meal verbs in order
  \item dinner takes an hour
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To have dinner? (\textbf{cenar}.) The meal itself? (\textbf{la cena}.) What else can \emph{comer} mean in Spain? (\textbf{To have lunch}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(decidir, coincidir, equivocarse …]{(decidir, coincidir, equivocarse, tardar, cenar) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R437-repaso-planes}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say all five: \emph{to decide}, \emph{to clash}, \emph{to get it wrong}, \emph{to take time}, \emph{to have dinner}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the reflexive marks what happens to you}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{plain} & \textbf{reflexive} & \textbf{the difference} \\
\midrule
decido & me decido & choosing a thing vs making up your mind \\
equivoco & \textbf{me equivoco} & the error befalls you \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{equivocarse} is almost never plain, because a mistake is something that happens \textbf{to} a person. The same shape covers \emph{caerse}, \emph{olvidarse} and \emph{perderse} — a family worth noticing together rather than one at a time.

\textbf{coincidir} takes no reflexive and still points at you: \emph{me coincide} uses the indirect pronoun, not the reflexive, because the clash is reported \textbf{to} you rather than done by you.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{Seven chapters ago you could name things. You can now arrange an evening and say what went wrong with it.} You can be offered two dates, decide, say the other one clashes, admit a mistake, say how long something takes and name the meal at the end of it.

\textbf{tardar} closes a debt: the chapter on delays mentioned it in passing and did not teach it, and a word shown but never given is one a reader half-knows.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all five words
  \item it clashes with work, so I have to decide
  \item they made a mistake with my order
  \item it takes an hour and we have dinner at nine
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To clash? (\textbf{coincidir}.) To get it wrong? (\textbf{equivocarse}.) To take time? (\textbf{tardar}.) To decide? (\textbf{decidir}.) To have dinner? (\textbf{cenar}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(cambiar un plan) — read it, then do it yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C437-sintesis-plan}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{coincidir} and \emph{decidir}. The message you are about to read turns on both.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Read it once straight through, then answer.

\begin{quote}
Hola: al final no puedo el jueves, me \textbf{coincide} con el curso. Perdona, me \textbf{equivoqué} de semana al apuntarlo. ¿\textbf{Cenamos} el viernes? Yo \textbf{tardo} media hora en llegar, así que sobre las nueve.
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item why Thursday is impossible
  \item what mistake the writer admits
  \item what is proposed instead, and at what time
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Now write the reply. Say aloud:

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Friday clashes with my class
  \item I got the week wrong too
  \item I take twenty minutes to get there
  \item let us decide now and have dinner on Saturday
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Every sentence there is an ordinary message between two friends}, and none of it was sayable seven chapters ago — not because the grammar was missing, but because the verbs were.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
It clashes? (\textbf{me coincide}.) I got it wrong? (\textbf{me equivoqué}.) Shall we have dinner? (\textbf{¿cenamos?})
\end{tcolorbox}
